title: Half-Life of Radioactive Waste
learningObjectives: Use the half-life equation to predict the amount of radioactive material remaining after a given time.
Compare short-lived fission products and long-lived transuranic waste in high-level waste.
Explain why high-level waste requires shielding and long-term management.

evidence.quote: Strontium-90 and cesium-137 have half-lives of about 30 years (half the radioactivity will decay in 30 years).

explanations.text: A half-life is the time for half the radioactivity to decay. After one half-life half remains, after two half-lives one quarter remains.

evidence.quote: These isotopes, called "fission products," account for most of the heat and penetrating radiation in high-level waste.
These heavier-than-uranium, or "transuranic," elements do not produce nearly the amount of heat

explanations.text: Fission products produce most heat and penetrating radiation, while heavier transuranic elements produce less heat but take much longer to decay.

evidence.quote: Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,000 years.
Transuranic wastes, sometimes called TRU, account for most of the radioactive hazard remaining in high-level waste after 1,000 years.

explanations.text: Some isotopes decay quickly, but plutonium-239 lasts tens of thousands of years, so transuranic waste remains hazardous after 1,000 years.
